opus-5.5.text:
I think it's because the company keeps changing underneath you, and if you don't change with it, you become the bottleneck.

When I started, I was basically a researcher and a programmer. My whole identity was writing code, designing systems, and thinking about compilers and computer graphics. That was what I was good at, and it was comfortable. But very quickly the company needed something else. Once you have a few people, you're no longer the person who writes the most code. You're the person who has to make sure everyone else can do their best work. That's a totally different skill. Then the team grows again, and suddenly you're thinking about hiring, culture, fundraising, talking to customers, product direction, and sales. Each stage asks you to be a different person.

What surprised me is how fast this happens. In academia you can stay the same kind of person for years and keep getting better at one thing. In a startup the environment shifts every few months. The market changes, especially in AI. The technology changes, your users change, and the size of the team changes. The approach that worked six months ago might be exactly the wrong approach now. If you keep doing what made you successful before, you can actually hurt the company.

So "reinventing yourself" for me means being willing to let go of the role you're comfortable with. Sometimes that's painful. As an engineer, you love solving technical problems yourself. But at some point the highest-leverage thing you can do is not write code. It's to find the right people, set the right direction, and make hard decisions quickly.

I also think the founder has to grow at least as fast as the company. If the company is growing faster than you are, you become the ceiling. So every few months I try to step back and ask: what does the company need from me now, and what do I need to stop doing? Honestly, the answer is usually uncomfortable, and that's how I know I'm on the right track.

r001.rationale: The response says founders must change as the company grows, but does not describe viewing one's three-month-earlier self as foolish.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the pace of startups with the stability of academia, but does not discuss startup survival pressure or school protecting people from that pressure.

r003.rationale: It describes shifting from technical work to leadership tasks, but does not say Yuanming integrates the strengths of academic and business mindsets.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it comes from my own experience rather than any theory. When I started Taichi, I was a PhD student. My identity was basically "researcher." I wrote papers, I wrote code, and I thought the hardest problem in the world was making a compiler generate fast kernels. Then suddenly I was a founder, and within a few months I realized that almost nothing I was good at was the thing the company needed most.

The first phase, you're really just an engineer who happens to have a company. You write most of the code yourself. Then you hire a few people, and now the bottleneck isn't your code, it's whether you can explain what you want clearly enough that someone else can build it. So you have to become a manager, and that's a totally different skill. I was really bad at it at first. I would just rewrite people's code instead of giving feedback, which is the worst thing you can do.

Then maybe six months later, the problem changes again. Now it's not about the product, it's about whether anyone actually wants it. So you have to become a salesperson, or a marketer, or someone who spends a lot of time talking to users and understanding what they're really trying to do. For a technical person this is very uncomfortable. I had to learn to listen more than I talk, which is not natural for me.

And then you raise money, and now you need to understand finance, hiring, legal, company culture, all these things. The company keeps growing, and every stage the thing that got you here is not the thing that gets you to the next stage. If you keep doing what you did in the previous stage, you actually become the bottleneck of the company.

So that's why I say three to six months. It's not that you choose to reinvent yourself, it's that the company grows faster than you do, and you have to keep catching up. The humbling part is that you're never really an expert at your current job. By the time you get decent at it, the job has changed. But I think that's also what makes it fun. You learn more in two years of doing a startup than in ten years of doing anything else.

r001.rationale: The response describes changing roles and learning quickly, but never says that seeing one’s three-month-earlier self as foolish signals growth.

r002.rationale: It mentions Hu’s PhD background and the demands of a startup, but does not contrast startup survival pressure with protection from that pressure in school.

r003.rationale: It describes moving from research and engineering into management, sales, and other roles, but does not present company leadership as integrating academic and business mindsets.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because the company changes so quickly that what makes you useful at one stage may become a bottleneck at the next stage. In the beginning, you might be writing code and solving technical problems yourself. Then you need to recruit people, communicate what you’re trying to build, and help the team make decisions without you being involved in everything.

That’s a very different job. If your instinct is always, “I can do this faster myself,” you can actually prevent the company from growing. You have to learn to get satisfaction from enabling other people to do great work.

So every three to six months, you need to ask yourself: What does the company need from me now? What should I stop doing? And what am I avoiding because I’m not good at it yet? The uncomfortable part is that you’re constantly becoming a beginner again. But I think that’s part of the job.

r002.rationale: It discusses startup growth pressure, but does not contrast it with protection from survival pressure in school.

r003.rationale: The response discusses adapting to a changing company role, but does not describe integrating academic and business mindsets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because the bottleneck keeps changing. When you start, the question is, can you build something that works? You spend most of your time writing code and solving technical problems. Then you need to figure out whether anyone actually wants it. That requires talking to users, listening carefully, and sometimes letting go of something you were very excited to build.

If that starts working, the challenge becomes hiring people and helping them work together. You can’t personally make every decision anymore. The thing that made you effective in the beginning—being able to do everything yourself—can actually become a limitation.

So every three to six months, you have to ask, what does the company need from me now? And am I spending my time on that, or am I doing something just because I’m good at it and it feels comfortable? That’s the reinvention. You’re still the same person, but you have to keep learning a different job.
